Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The performance of infectious disease forecasting models is commonly calculated under the implicit assumption that forecast accuracy is equally important across time.
This approach may obscure or under-weight differences in model performance during the epidemic periods that matter most for public-health decisions.
Here, we introduce the weighted prequential score (WPS), a forecast evaluation framework that can emphasize epidemic periods of interest.

The WPS is a weighted average of scores over time, where weights are constructed through entropic tilting which up-weights priority periods while keeping the WPS as close as possible to the arithmetic average.

We demonstrate the WPS on forecasts of incident hospitalizations submitted to the CDC FluSight challenge, focusing on two priority periods: weeks of rapid growth in incidence and weeks near the seasonal peak.

Across season-location-horizon pairs, doubling the weight assigned to priority periods changes the top-ranked model in 10%-26% of eligible settings, while the top-ranked model remains unchanged regardless of the amount of weight assigned in 37%-68% of settings.

We demonstrate that for suitable weights, the models favored by the WPS yield an average gain in accuracy during priority periods that is at least as large as the average accuracy lost during the remaining weeks.
Because weights can be defined using observed outcomes, the WPS is not a proper scoring rule.
Hence, we recommend using the WPS as a retrospective evaluation diagnostic.

The WPS can guide public-health practitioners in selecting models that perform well during periods most relevant to their decisions, while encouraging forecasting teams to improve accuracy during these critical weeks.
Quantitative evaluation of probabilistic forecasts of infectious disease incidence requires a scoring rule.
In infectious disease modeling, commonly used rules include the weighted interval score (WIS) [1, 2], continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) [3, 4], and logarithmic score [5, 6].

text.text: Here, we introduce the weighted prequential score (WPS), a scoring rule that allows emphasis on forecast performance during designated periods.

text.text: In this section, we introduce the weighted prequential score (WPS) and derived quantities that summarize its effect on model ranking.
For simplicity, we describe our method assuming single-week-ahead forecasts, although it generalizes to any forecast horizon.
Let Y 1:T = (Y 1 , . . . , Y T ) be a sequence of weekly observations over a season of duration T weeks (e.g., incident hospitalization counts during a flu season).
Each week, a forecaster issues a forecast distribution P t for Y t using information available up to week t -1.
We denote the score of this forecast by S(P t , y t ), where S is a proper score, such as the WIS or CRPS, and y t is the observed count.
A common way to evaluate model forecast performance is using the arithmetic average of the scores (see e.g., [2, 8]).
text.formatted: A common way to evaluate model forecast performance is using the arithmetic average of the scores (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>).

text.text: We refer to this score as the prequential score (PS) as in Dawid and Musio [11]: S(P 1:T , y 1:T ) := 1 T T t=1 S(P t , y t ).
text.formatted: We refer to this score as the prequential score (PS) as in Dawid and Musio <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>: S(P 1:T , y 1:T ) := 1 T T t=1 S(P t , y t ).

text.text: Here, we propose to instead evaluate forecasts using the weighted prequential score (WPS), Sπ (P 1:T , y 1:T ) := T t=1 π(t; y 1:T )S(P t , y t ), where π(t; y 1:T ) is the weight for time t depending on the observed sequence y 1:T .
Note that the PS is a special case where the weight distribution is uniform π 0 (t) ≡ 1/T.
For simplicity, we choose a binary rule for assigning weights to forecast-observation pairs, but our approach can be extended to more flexible weighting rules (see Supplementary Material).
In particular, a set of event weeks E is assigned a higher weight relative to weeks in the non-event week set E c .
Specifically, the user selects an emphasis ratio r ≥ 1 that determines how strongly the evaluation prioritizes accuracy during the event weeks relative to the rest of the season.
Setting r > 1 emphasizes accuracy on weeks in E relative to the PS, while r = 1 recovers the PS.

Importantly, it requires only a definition of event weeks and the emphasis ratio, r, making it particularly useful when an explicit utility function is difficult to specify.

We demonstrated on the CDC FluSight challenge that the WPS is a flexible method to underscore priority periods in model evaluation, and that under suitable weights it selects models whose improvements during event weeks exceed losses during non-event weeks.
The WPS is closely related to existing scoring rules that connect the quality of a forecast to its value for public health decision making.

Notably, Gerding et al. [15] derive a proper scoring rule that evaluates forecasts based on their ability to effectively allocate limited medical resources; Marshall et al. [16] propose a modification of WIS that normalizes and caps the interval score according to a utility-based error tolerance.

text.text: These approaches provide a valuable framework for connecting a given scoring rule to an explicit utility function.
The WPS takes a complementary approach by changing how an unmodified score is aggregated over a season.
The benefit of this approach is that neither a loss function nor a utility threshold needs to be defined explicitly, as these may be difficult to define or elicit.
Both strategies are nonetheless closely related, since a utility-based scoring function implicitly emphasizes a particular set of weeks.

For example, the allocation score is largest when incidence is close to the amount of available resources, which in the application of Gerding et al. occurred during the growth and decline periods of the epidemic curve [15].

text.text: This approach results in a proper scoring rule which mitigates the influence of high-incidence weeks or highly populated locations on the aggregate seasonal score.

At the expense of propriety, the WPS can achieve a similar effect for an appropriately defined set of event weeks, additionally allowing more control over the amount of emphasis (e.g., giving more weight to less populated locations while still emphasizing performance on high incidence weeks).
The main limitation of the WPS is that, when weights depend on observed outcomes, it is not proper for the true joint data-generating distribution.
Instead, the WPS incentivizes forecasters to assign higher probability to outcome sequences that receive larger weight under the WPS.

This issue is closely related to the forecaster's dilemma identified by Lerch et al. [17], who showed that when evaluation is restricted to extreme observations, forecasters do not need to be skillful with respect to the true data-generating distribution.

By allowing users to explicitly prioritize the weeks most important to their decisions, the WPS provides a flexible framework that makes the temporal priorities underlying aggregate evaluation explicit and better connects predictive performance to its downstream value for decision making.
Consequently, we recommend using the WPS with moderate weighting alongside proper scoring rules to support November 12, 2026 11/17 model selection that better reflects public-health priorities.
